about: Kinds of translation decision that tend to be changed after the fact: overridden at the style questionnaire, corrected at an approval gate, or relitigated through judge false positives and reader notes. A planned decisions scan (not built yet) is to read each chapter against this list and propose decision cards. `detection_cues` are what to look for in the English source; `lands_in` is the artifact a ruling updates. A category may carry `house_default`, the answer you give in every book: the scan is to propose it as the recommendation and ask only if the book gives a reason to depart. This is the shipped sample, with invented examples and no house defaults. Copy it to prompts/decisions_taxonomy.json and grow it from your own books (scripts/decision_archaeology.py mines them); tag each example with its `project` so a replay can hold that book's own examples out. Nothing loads this file yet; for now it is reference data you read by hand.

categories.name: tú / usted between particular characters
categories.description: Who says tú or usted to whom, where the general rule does not settle it: servants and staff, shopkeepers, social hierarchies among animals, feudal courts, strangers, criminals, deliberate distancing, public versus private settings.
detection_cues: dialogue across a gap in age, rank, or familiarity
vocatives that mark status: sir, ma'am, my lord, boss, major, miss
servants, gardeners, shopkeepers, officials or captors who speak to the main characters
the same pair speaking both in private and before others
animal or non-human characters with an implied pecking order

examples.text: A gardener addressing the family's children: usted with señorita, while the children use tú back.
A prince and his father the king: usted at court, tú only when they are alone.

categories.name: Address that changes as the story moves
categories.description: A pair's form of address changes at an event: a family tie revealed, a death, a marriage, growing up, a change of rank. The map needs since/until/after_event rules instead of one default.
detection_cues: revelations of kinship or identity late in the book
time skips, coming of age, change of station
a character who is a stranger early and intimate later

examples.text: Two adults learn in the last chapters that they are cousins; their usted becomes tú from that scene on.

categories.name: Singular or plural address; whom the narrator speaks to
categories.description: Whether 'you' is one listener or several, and how a narrator or teacher addresses the reader: tú, ustedes, or usted. Includes group teaching and lesson-book voices.
detection_cues: a narrator or teacher speaking directly to the reader
a speaker addressing a group, a class, or 'you all'
lesson-book or catechism formats

examples.text: A lesson book whose teacher speaks to 'you' throughout: one pupil (tú) or the class (ustedes)?

categories.name: Which names to translate
categories.description: Personal names, animal names, epithets and bynames, places (real and invented-descriptive), boats and ships, and placeholder names. The rule varies by book and must be stated so it can be applied consistently to every name, not decided one by one.
detection_cues: names that are ordinary English words (Thunder, Blackrock Island, Old Grey)
the text explaining or playing on a name
epithets of the form 'X the Y' or 'X of the Y'
historical or saga names with established Spanish forms
generic stand-in names in examples or parables (Mr. Smith)

examples.text: A horse called Thunder and a dog called Rex in the same book: translate descriptive names only, or none?
An invented 'Crooked Creek': translate by its common noun (arroyo Torcido) or keep the English?

categories.name: Titles, honorifics and kinship terms with names
categories.description: How a title combines with a name in narration and in direct address, and which titles are translated: Mr., Mrs., Miss, Aunt, Grandpa, Doc, Dame, Monsignor, military and religious ranks.
detection_cues: Title + surname or kinship + given name
foreign or archaic honorifics
titles used alone as vocatives

examples.text: Mr. Brown in narration and in speech: el señor Brown, Sr. Brown, or Mr. Brown?

categories.name: A figure's sex where Spanish must mark it
categories.description: Spanish nouns, adjectives and pronouns force a sex that English can leave open: animals of a stated or unstated sex, epicene species, babies, characters whose sex is unknown or disguised, and sex-neutral terms (yearling, foal) that have no neutral Spanish form.
detection_cues: animal characters, especially named ones and species words like kitten, goose, colt
'it' or no pronoun for a baby or a creature
disguise, cross-dressing, or mistaken-identity plots
a sex revealed only later in the book

examples.text: A kitten called only 'it' until chapter 9 reveals she is female: gatito or gatita from the start?

categories.name: Terms already settled in sibling books
categories.description: Vocabulary already fixed in other books of the same domain or series, or in a prequel. A fresh choice relitigates it.
detection_cues: the book shares a domain with existing projects
a sequel or series volume
terms the glossary of a sibling book already carries

examples.text: A sequel that uses 'stall' throughout, where the first volume's glossary already chose one rendering.

categories.name: Technical, regional and natural-history terms
categories.description: Species, plants, trades, ranching, sailing, science: the Spanish has several candidates that differ by region or precision. Verify against web sources rather than model memory.
detection_cues: species and plant names, especially regional or foreign ones
trade or technical vocabulary repeated through the book
science or nature writing

examples.text: 'spruce' in a forest setting: the botanically precise word or the one readers know?

categories.name: How hard the Spanish vocabulary may be
categories.description: How far word choice can stretch for the audience: rare, regional or bookish words a young reader stumbles on. Includes words the story itself discusses, whose Spanish must be equally hard.
detection_cues: the target reader's age
a character asking what a word means, or mispronouncing it
dense regional or period vocabulary

examples.text: A child character asks what 'ambidextrous' means: the Spanish word must puzzle a child too.

categories.name: Dialect, slang, archaism and narrative register
categories.description: How eye-dialect, period slang, archaic speech and the narrator's register are carried into Spanish.
detection_cues: apostrophe-dropped spellings (hoss, yuh, 'tisn't)
period slang and exclamations
thee/thou, archaic syntax, a deliberately elevated narrator

examples.text: A ranch hand who says 'I reckon yuh ain't seen him': dialect spelling, or colloquial vocabulary in standard spelling?

categories.name: Wordplay that lands only in English
categories.description: Puns, letter games, name jokes, rhymes and jokes that depend on English words. Each instance needs its own decision; a book that depends on them throughout may not be worth translating.
detection_cues: puns and homophones, a joke explained in the text
acrostics and letter-based games
names whose meaning carries a joke
rhymed taunts and nonsense verse

examples.text: An alphabet rhyme ('A was an apple'): adapt each line to a Spanish word with the same letter.

categories.name: Quoted verse, songs, scripture and published works
categories.description: Poems, songs, hymns, scripture and quotations from other books: whether a public-domain Spanish translation exists, whether to write a new one, prose or verse, and which Bible version and citation format.
detection_cues: lineated verse, song lyrics, hymn titles
scripture quotations and references
quotations attributed to other authors

examples.text: Characters sing two verses of a well-known hymn: use an existing Spanish version or translate the English?

categories.name: Religion, disability, ethnicity and period attitudes
categories.description: Religious interjections, disability terms, ethnic labels and period attitudes: how faithfully to render them, and never to add what the English does not carry.
detection_cues: interjections and oaths, religious or not
terms for disability, race or ethnicity
period attitudes the narrator voices

examples.text: 'Oh dear!' rendered as '¡Dios mío!' adds a religious note the English does not carry.

categories.name: Measurements, money and cultural references
categories.description: Units, currency, school grades, holidays, foods and institutions of the source culture: keep, convert or adapt.
detection_cues: miles, feet, pounds, dollars
school grades, holidays, period institutions

examples.text: 'Ten miles to town' and 'two bits': keep miles and American coins, or convert?

categories.name: Nested speech, emphasis and other typography
categories.description: Speech inside framed stories, thoughts versus speech, letters, and typographic emphasis (italics, capitals): book-specific conventions the dialogue judge must know.
detection_cues: a character telling a story with quoted dialogue inside it
italic or capital emphasis in speech
letters, signs, inscriptions

examples.text: A grandfather tells a story in which his characters speak: raya inside raya, or guillemets for the inner speech?
